title: Needs and wants
job: Say what you want and don't want
verifiedBy: Fable (Claude Fable 5) — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: What you want follows the verb in the order English expects: urīd ʿaṣīr, lā urīd al-ḥalīb. Nothing moves in a want, a refusal or a question — hal (M2) still just sits in front.

Negation is one word in front of the verb and nothing else changes: urīd → lā urīd. English cannot say "I not want" — it has to bring in "do" — and that auxiliary has no Arabic counterpart. The lā is M2's word for "no", doing its second job.

lā negates a VERB only. A sentence with no verb in it — anā ṭālib — would need a different word (laysa) to say "I am not", and L1 never teaches it. So every "not" in this module sits on a verb, and "I am not…" waits.

Wanting to DO something is urīd an + a second, fully conjugated verb: urīd an ashrab al-qahwa — "I want that I-drink the-coffee". There is no infinitive, no "to drink", to reach for: an is obligatory, and the verb after it still carries its own person prefix.

Both English-shaped shortcuts fail: urīd ashrab drops the an that English never had, and urīd an yashrab keeps the an but lets the person slip to "he". Both verbs say I, so both wear the first-person prefix: urīd an ashrab.

The adjective FOLLOWS its noun and agrees with it twice — in gender AND in definiteness. The second agreement is the difference between a phrase and a sentence: bayt kabīr (a big house) · al-bayt al-kabīr (the big house) · al-bayt kabīr (the house IS big).
Feminine agreement puts -a on the adjective: qahwa sākhina, sayyāra kabīra — the same -a that M1 put on ṭāliba, now tracking a noun instead of a person.

turīd is BOTH "you want" (to a man) AND "she wants" — the tu- prefix does double duty, and English never collides these two. "You want" said to a woman is turīdīn: the -īn tail, not the prefix, is what carries her.

The slogan to drop: "add -a to make it feminine". Gender belongs to the NOUN and is learned with it — al-Hind is feminine with no -a in sight. What -a reliably marks is the word that AGREES: the adjective here, the verb's turīdīn tail, and in M8 the number.

words.note: Juice. Bare in a request — urīd ʿaṣīr — exactly like M1's urīd qahwa; with the article, al-ʿaṣīr is that particular juice. The ʿ is ʿayn, the squeeze deep in the throat, and ṣ is the heavy s.

sentences.trap: A request stays bare: urīd ʿaṣīr, no al-. Put the article on and you are pointing at one particular glass — M1's law, still running.
sentences.sound: u-REED ʿa-ṢEER — the ʿ is a squeeze deep in the throat, and ṣ a heavy s with the tongue low.

variations.changed: add al- — that particular juice, the one in view
swap the drink — the request stays bare

variations.cue: Do you want a juice? (to a man)
variations.changed: the request turned into the offer — hal in front, and tu- for you

mistake.why: wāḥid is the number one, not English's "a". Arabic has no indefinite article: a request is just urīd ʿaṣīr.

sentences.usage: Ordering at a café or a juice stall — direct and normal.
sentences.mnemonic: ʿaṣīr is the squeezed thing — ʿaṣara, to press. Juice is what the press gives you.

words.note: ḥalīb is milk; al-ḥalīb is milk with its article on. Refusing milk in general keeps al- — lā urīd al-ḥalīb — M1's law again: a statement about the whole class keeps the article English drops.

sentences.trap: The refusal keeps the al- that a request would drop: milk in general is al-ḥalīb. English says "I don't want milk" bare; Arabic does not.
sentences.sound: laa u-REED al-ḥa-LEEB — laa long and flat, ḥ the hard breathy h.

variations.changed: milk → tea — the general statement keeps its article, sun-letter spelling and all
want → like: the same lā sits in front of any verb
the refusal undone — and the request drops the al- the refusal kept

mistake.why: English can say "I want no milk", hanging the no on the noun. lā negates the verb and stands in front of it: lā urīd al-ḥalīb.

sentences.usage: Refusing what is offered, or ordering without — milk in the coffee is the everyday case.
sentences.mnemonic: ḥalīb comes from the verb "to milk": the milked-thing.

words.note: No English translation, obligatory between urīd and a second verb: urīd an ashrab, "I want that I-drink". There is no infinitive, so an is the hinge; the verb after it keeps its person.
The verb "drink" with a- on the front: the a- is "I", the same person-prefix law as uḥibb and urīd (those take u- because of their shape). tashrab, yashrab arrive with M4; here every drinker is I.

sentences.trap: "Want to drink" has an infinitive in English and none in Arabic: an, plus a verb that still says who is drinking.
sentences.sound: u-REED an ASH-rab al-QAH-wa — an is short and unstressed, run straight into the verb.

variations.cue: I want to drink some water
variations.changed: coffee → water, and bare: this one is a request

variations.cue: I don't want to drink coffee
variations.changed: lā in front of urīd — the first verb is the one negated

variations.cue: I want to drink a hot coffee
variations.changed: the an-frame carries a whole request — bare qahwa, and sākhina agreeing behind it

mistake.why: Two verbs cannot touch. English "I want to drink" has an infinitive; Arabic has an: urīd an ashrab. Dropping it is the commonest English-shaped slip in the level.

sentences.usage: Wanting to do, not to have — the frame every later "want to" sentence uses.
sentences.mnemonic: an is the hinge: want THAT I-drink — two verbs, one small pin between them.

sentences.cue: Do you want a coffee? (to a man)

words.note: The tu- prefix does double duty: turīd is "you want" (to a man) AND "she wants" — English never collides those two. yurīd is "he wants". Asking a woman needs one more piece, the -īn tail: turīdīn.

sentences.trap: There is no "do" to build the question with. hal in front, and the tu- of turīd already holds the you.
sentences.sound: hal tu-REED QAH-wa — the question is carried by hal; the voice rises only a little.

variations.cue: Do you want water? (to a man)
variations.changed: swap what is offered — hal turīd holds still
tu- → yu-: he, and it is a statement again
drop hal and nothing else: the same turīd now reads "she wants" — the double duty the row warns about

mistake.why: The tu- already says you. anta on top is emphasis — "do YOU want a coffee?" — not the neutral offer.

sentences.usage: Offering — the host's question. Gendered like every "you" since M2: this one is to a man.
sentences.mnemonic: turīd — the tu- turns the wanting onto you (or onto her: one prefix, two owners).

words.note: "Only", and it follows what it limits, sitting at the end: urīd māʾ faqaṭ — "I want water, that's all". English puts "just" in front; faqaṭ closes the sentence instead.

sentences.trap: "Just" goes at the front in English and at the back in Arabic: māʾ faqaṭ.
sentences.sound: laa, u-REED MAAʾ fa-QAṬ — the little stop of māʾ, then faqaṭ with its heavy ṭ.

variations.changed: the shortest polite refusal — no verb needed at all
swap what is limited — faqaṭ stays at the end
the refusal becomes an acceptance — naʿam, and faqaṭ still closes it

mistake.why: English puts "just" before the noun. faqaṭ follows what it limits, at the end of the sentence: urīd māʾ faqaṭ.

sentences.usage: Turning an offer down and keeping it simple.
sentences.mnemonic: faqaṭ ends the list the way a full stop ends a sentence: that, and only that.

sentences.cue: Do you want tea? (to a woman)

words.note: "You want" to a woman: turīd plus the -īn tail. tu- alone is you-m or she, so the ending carries her. The -īn is written because it is the person; MSA's turīdīna adds a mood vowel this course drops.

sentences.trap: One question, two shapes: hal turīd to a man, hal turīdīn to a woman. English asks both with one sentence.
sentences.sound: hal tu-ree-DEEN SHAAY — the -īn is a full long syllable and takes the stress.

variations.cue: Do you want a coffee? (to a woman)
variations.changed: swap the drink — the -īn stays

variations.cue: Do you want a coffee? (to a man)
variations.changed: asked of a man — the tail goes
her answer: the -īn was the asking shape — the I-form urīd has no tail

mistake.why: anti names a woman, but turīd without its tail asks a man. The verb, not the pronoun, has to carry her: hal turīdīn shāy?

sentences.usage: The same offer, to a woman — the tail is not optional.
sentences.mnemonic: To a woman the question grows a tail: turīd-īn.

sentences.cue: Yes, I want a hot coffee

words.note: "Hot", agreeing with qahwa: the adjective follows its noun and takes -a because qahwa is feminine — the -a of ṭāliba, now on a word describing a thing. Of a masculine noun it is bare: shāy sākhin.

sentences.trap: Two agreements at once: the adjective comes AFTER its noun, and it wears -a because qahwa is feminine.
sentences.sound: QAH-wa saa-KHI-na — kh is the ch of Scottish loch.

variations.changed: shāy is masculine — the adjective drops its -a
drop the adjective — the plain acceptance

variations.cue: Do you want a hot coffee? (to a woman)
variations.changed: the acceptance turned back into the offer — and sākhina still follows qahwa, not the woman asked

mistake.why: English adjectives never change shape, so nothing in English warns that the -a is missing. qahwa is feminine and its adjective follows it in gender: sākhina.

sentences.usage: Asking for it the way you want it — temperature, size: the adjective slot does the work.
sentences.mnemonic: sākhin sounds like sauna — heat either way.

words.note: "Very", and it FOLLOWS its adjective: sākhina jiddan, kabīr jiddan. English puts very first. The -an on its tail is the adverb ending this course writes out, as in shukran and kathīran.

sentences.trap: al-qahwa sākhina is a whole sentence — definite noun, bare adjective, no "is" anywhere. The Arabic sentence hides inside the English phrase.
sentences.sound: al-QAH-wa saa-KHI-na JID-dan — hold the doubled d of jiddan.

variations.changed: tea, masculine — no -a, and still no "is"
drop jiddan — the plain statement
hal in front of the verbless sentence: a question with no verb to lean on

mistake.why: English "very hot" puts very first. jiddan follows its adjective: sākhina jiddan.

sentences.usage: Complaint or praise — saying how the thing in front of you is.
sentences.mnemonic: jiddan doubles its d the way English doubles the word: very, very.

words.note: "Car", a feminine noun — its adjective takes the -a: sayyāra kabīra. With the article, the s swallows the l of al-: as-sayyāra, a sun letter doing what M2's ash-shāy did.
"Big", agreeing twice over: -a for a feminine noun (sayyāra kabīra), bare for a masculine one (bayt kabīr) — and when the noun is definite, the adjective puts on al- too: al-bayt al-kabīr.

sentences.trap: sayyāra kabīra — noun first, then the adjective agreeing in the feminine. English order, reversed.
sentences.sound: say-YAA-ra ka-BEE-ra — hold the doubled y of sayyāra.

variations.changed: drop the adjective — the bare want
add the article to the noun only — now it is a whole sentence
a masculine noun in the same want — and the adjective drops its -a to follow it

mistake.why: The English order. The adjective FOLLOWS its noun in Arabic: sayyāra kabīra.

sentences.usage: Wanting things, not just drinks — the frame is the same at any size.
sentences.mnemonic: sayyāra is the mover — from sāra, to travel.

words.note: bayt is house, al-bayt the house — b is a moon letter, so al- keeps its l. al-bayt also does the work of "home": M5 will say kuntu fī al-bayt, "I was at home".

sentences.trap: "The big house" needs TWO al-: al-bayt al-kabīr. The adjective agrees in definiteness too, not just gender.
sentences.sound: al-BAYT al-ka-BEER — two al-, both keeping their l: b and k are moon letters.

variations.changed: drop the adjective's al- — and the phrase becomes a whole sentence
house → car: the whole phrase agrees, feminine and definite

variations.cue: Do you want the big house? (to a man)
variations.changed: the choice offered instead of stated — hal, tu-, and both al- stay on

mistake.why: One al- is not enough inside a definite phrase: al-bayt kabīr is a whole sentence, "the house is big". The big house — one thing, pointed at — is al-bayt al-kabīr, agreement and all.

sentences.usage: Choosing between options — THE big one, already in view.
sentences.mnemonic: kabīr — big, as in the poet Kabir, "the great".
